inlines.text: 为什么要因为下半身的事把黄仁勋推出去背锅？

blocks.text: 有意思。首先，我周一问“黄仁勋还在跟谁上床？”的时候，可没指望这么快就有答案——有人，可能是董事会里的人（就像我们在其他事件中看到的那样），想让这件事传出去。其次，为什么要因为下半身的事把黄仁勋推出去背锅？这个行业根本不在乎这种事——问问 Eric Schmidt 和 Bill Gates 就知道了。我猜第二桩婚外情只是个动手的借口，这一切都要回到上周最初的那篇报道：黄仁勋被一名疑似中国间谍设了美人计。新云公司 Megaspeed 那边到底发生了什么，可能比我们知道的严重得多，而我们已知的部分就已经够糟了：商业登记信息指向的，是“一座马来西亚数据中心和购物中心、一间几乎空无一人的新加坡办公室，以及吉隆坡郊外一个破败的店面”。

blocks.text: 我认为 Megaspeed 只是冰山一角。与中国芯片相关的两起丑闻都可能给英伟达带来严重麻烦，而且两起事件的关键人物都与黄仁勋关系密切。其一是 Megaspeed，牵涉黄仁勋那位可能是间谍的情人。其二则围绕 Super Micro（其商号为 Supermicro，这名字实在糟糕）展开——这家英伟达的合作伙伴由黄仁勋的老友梁见后执掌。Super Micro 联合创始人廖益贤（Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw），以及张瑞沧（Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang）和孙廷伟（Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun），涉嫌欺诈美国，充当一家幌子公司的中转渠道，为阿里巴巴采购了价值 25 亿美元的英伟达芯片。据彭博社报道，这家起诉书中未点名的幌子公司是总部位于泰国的 OBON。梁见后和 Super Micro 均未被起诉。

blocks.text: 到了明年一月，伊丽莎白·沃伦将以参议院银行委员会主席的身份发出传票。而巧的是，她似乎对此相当感兴趣。民主党将同时掌控众议院和参议院。选民赋予了他们铲除腐败的使命。而天哪，英伟达现在看起来简直像一只待宰的鸭子。如果黄仁勋知道芯片被转移——或有理由知道——却仍设法确保销售，他可能已经犯下了实实在在的罪行（贿赂、间谍、走私，诸如此类），在一个正常运转的法律体系下，他真有可能进监狱。英伟达舍弃其不可或缺的 CEO，是在降低自己被卷入黄仁勋风波的风险。

blocks.text: Will it be that easy for Nvidia? I wonder. The most interesting part of the second affair story, with Powell, the Nvidia vice president of healthcare, comes at the very end of the New York Times article. When someone took a video of Powell and Huang being “affectionate” in March, Huang’s security had nondisclosure agreements ready to go. CNBC reports that rumors of their affair have circulated “for years.” I wonder what else was an open secret at the company, you know? Especially since Huang had 60 direct reports, so every part of the company is covered in his fingerprints.

blocks.text: Why throw Huang under the bus for getting his nuts drained?

inlines.text: Why throw Huang under the bus for getting his nuts drained?

blocks.text: Fascinating. First of all, when I asked on Monday “Who else is Jensen Huang fucking?” I did not expect to get answers this fast — somebody, potentially somebody on the board (as we’ve seen in other incidents), wanted the story out there. Second, why throw Huang under the bus for getting his nuts drained? This is not an industry that cares about that kind of thing — just ask Eric Schmidt and Bill Gates. My guess is that the second affair is a pretext for action, and this all goes back to the original story from last week: that Huang was honeypotted by an alleged Chinese spy. Whatever was going on with neocloud Megaspeed might be much, much worse than we know, and what we know is pretty bad: business listings that led to “a Malaysian data center and shopping mall, a near-empty office in Singapore and a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur.”

blocks.text: Even months before the report that Alice “No Relation” Huang, an exec at Megaspeed, was having an affair with Huang, there were questions about Nvidia’s business in China. The US government has placed strict export controls on Nvidia’s high-end chips. Huang claimed in May that as a result, Nvidia has zero percent market share in China. But also in May, short sellers Culper Research published a report in which they wrote, “We believe that in reality, over 20% of Nvidia’s FY 2026 compute revenues remained driven by China – supported both by illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries.”

blocks.text: Megaspeed is only part of the story, I think. There are two Chinese chip-related scandals that could cause serious problems for Nvidia, and both feature people with close ties to Huang. One is Megaspeed, which involves Huang’s maybe-spy affair partner. The other centers on Super Micro (which, horribly, does business as Supermicro), a partner of Nvidia run by one of Huang’s old friends, Charles Liang. Super Micro’s cofounder, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, along with Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang and Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, allegedly defrauded the US by serving as a passthrough for a front company to buy $2.5 billion of Nvidia chips for Alibaba. The front company, not named in the indictment, is Thailand-based OBON, according to Bloomberg. Liang and Super Micro have not been charged.

Democrats will control both the House and the Senate. Their voters have given them a mandate to root out corruption. And boy howdy, does Nvidia look like a sitting duck right now. If Huang knew chips were being diverted — or had reason to know that — and tried to ensure their sales anyway, he may have committed actual crimes (bribery, espionage, smuggling, whatever) and, under a functioning legal system, could actually go to jail. Nvidia dispensing with its indispensable CEO is the company reducing its risk of getting roped into Huang’s drama.

The most interesting part of the second affair story, with Powell, the Nvidia vice president of healthcare, comes at the very end of the New York Times article. When someone took a video of Powell and Huang being “affectionate” in March, Huang’s security had nondisclosure agreements ready to go. CNBC reports that rumors of their affair have circulated “for years.” I wonder what else was an open secret at the company, you know? Especially since Huang had 60 direct reports, so every part of the company is covered in his fingerprints.
